pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
> 📊 **Strand 4 — Handling Data**
Collecting, organising, presenting and interpreting information to make good decisions.

> 🎯 **Content standard** (B9.4.2)
- B9.4.2.1 — Identify the sample space for a probability experiment involving two dependent events and express the probabilities of given events as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios to solve problems.

> 🎯 **In this chapter you will learn to:**
- perform experiments without replacement and list sample spaces
- recognise dependent events
- draw tree diagrams for dependent events and calculate probabilities
- solve problems using a standard deck of playing cards

pages.title: Experiments without replacement
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Perform a probability experiment involving two dependent events, e.g. drawing coloured bottle tops from a bag without replacement.
Curriculum indicator B9.4.2.1.1
> 🔑 **Key idea: Dependent events** — Events are **dependent** when the outcome of one **changes** the probabilities of the other. Picking objects **without replacement** gives dependent events, because each pick changes what is left in the bag.
## ✏️ Example 15.1
In an experiment, Anita picks one bottle top at a time, three times, from a bag containing 3 red (R), 2 green (G) and 1 pink (P) bottle tops, without replacement.
a) List the elements of the sample space. b) Does the outcome of one trial affect the others?
**Solution**
a) Each outcome is an ordered list of three colours. Because there is only 1 pink, P cannot appear twice:
Listed systematically, there are 19 possible orders:
| RRR | RRG | RRP | RGR | RGG |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| RGP | RPR | RPG | GRR | GRG |
| GRP | GGR | GGP | GPR | GPG |
| PRR | PRG | PGR | PGG |  |
Outcomes such as GGG and PPx are **impossible** — there are only 2 green and 1 pink.
b) **Yes.** For example, P(red on the 1st pick) = [[3/6]], but if a red is taken, P(red on the 2nd pick) = [[2/5]]. The trials are **dependent**.
> ✏️ **Practice:** Exercise 15.1, at the end of section 15.2, covers this section too. Tap **Quick check** to try its questions.

questions.q: Explain why "tossing a coin twice" gives independent events but "picking two learners from a class to be prefects" gives dependent events.

parts.a: A coin has the same chances on every toss. Once one learner is chosen, they cannot be chosen again, so the choices left (and the probabilities) change.

pages.title: Tree diagrams for dependent events
pages.body:
> 🎯 **You will learn to:** Express the probabilities of the events as fractions, decimals, percentages and/or ratios, e.g. using a tree diagram, table or another graphic organiser.
Curriculum indicator B9.4.2.1.2
> 🔑 **Key idea: Multiplication rule for dependent events** — P(A and then B) = P(A) × P(B **given that** A has happened). On a tree diagram, the probabilities on the second set of branches change according to what happened on the first branch.
## ✏️ Example 15.2
Draw a tree diagram for the first two picks in Anita's experiment (3 R, 2 G, 1 P, without replacement). Express the probabilities of the outcomes as fractions, decimals, percentages and ratios.
**Solution**
[[fig:m9-f39]]
Figure 15.1: Two picks without replacement
| **Outcome** | **Calculation** | **Fraction** | **Decimal** | **Percentage** | **Ratio** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| RR | [[3/6]] × [[2/5]] | [[6/30]] = [[1/5]] | 0.2 | 20% | 1 : 5 |
| RG | [[3/6]] × [[2/5]] | [[1/5]] | 0.2 | 20% | 1 : 5 |
| RP | [[3/6]] × [[1/5]] | [[1/10]] | 0.1 | 10% | 1 : 10 |
| GR | [[2/6]] × [[3/5]] | [[1/5]] | 0.2 | 20% | 1 : 5 |
| GG | [[2/6]] × [[1/5]] | [[1/15]] | 0.067 | 6.7% | 1 : 15 |
| GP | [[2/6]] × [[1/5]] | [[1/15]] | 0.067 | 6.7% | 1 : 15 |
| PR | [[1/6]] × [[3/5]] | [[1/10]] | 0.1 | 10% | 1 : 10 |
| PG | [[1/6]] × [[2/5]] | [[1/15]] | 0.067 | 6.7% | 1 : 15 |
| Total |  | 1 | 1 | 100% |  |
For example, P(two tops of the same colour) = P(RR) + P(GG) = [[1/5]] + [[1/15]] = [[4/15]] ≈ 26.7%.

pages.title: Playing cards
pages.body:
## Playing cards
> 🔑 **Key idea: A standard deck** — A standard deck has **52 cards** in 4 suits (♠ spades, ♥ hearts, ♦ diamonds, ♣ clubs) of 13 cards each: Ace, 2–10, Jack, Queen, King. There are **4 Aces**, 4 Jacks, 4 Queens and 4 Kings.
## ✏️ Example 15.3
Two cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find the probability of drawing a) two Aces b) an Ace and then a Jack. Express each answer as a fraction, decimal, percentage and ratio.
**Solution**
a) P(Ace first) = [[4/52]]. One Ace has gone, so P(Ace second) = [[3/51]].
P(two Aces) = [[4/52]] × [[3/51]] = [[12/2652]] = [[1/221]] ≈ 0.0045 ≈ 0.45% (ratio 1 : 221)
b) P(Ace first) = [[4/52]]. All 4 Jacks remain among 51 cards: P(Jack second) = [[4/51]].
P(Ace then Jack) = [[4/52]] × [[4/51]] = [[16/2652]] = [[4/663]] ≈ 0.0060 ≈ 0.60% (ratio 4 : 663)
> ✨ **Did you know?** Compare with replacement: P(two Aces) would be [[4/52]] × [[4/52]] = [[1/169]] ≈ 0.59% — a little more likely, because the Ace is put back.

pages.title: Exercise 15.1
pages.body:
> ✏️ **Exercise 15.1** — try these on paper or in your head, then tap **Quick check** to see the answers.
1. A bag contains 4 white and 3 black balls. Two balls are taken without replacement. Draw a tree diagram and find: a) P(both white) b) P(both black) c) P(one of each colour). Give answers as fractions and percentages.
2. A box contains 5 good and 2 faulty bulbs. Two are selected at random without replacement. Find the probability that a) both are faulty b) at least one is good.
3. Two cards are drawn without replacement from a standard deck. Find the probability that: a) both are hearts b) the first is a King and the second a Queen c) both are red.
4. Explain why "tossing a coin twice" gives independent events but "picking two learners from a class to be prefects" gives dependent events.

pages.title: Chapter 15 summary
pages.body:
- Dependent events: one outcome changes the probabilities of the next (e.g. without replacement).
- P(A then B) = P(A) × P(B after A); on a tree, the second-stage probabilities depend on the first branch.
- Express answers as fractions, decimals, percentages or ratios.

questions.q: A class has 12 boys and 18 girls. Two learners are chosen at random to represent the class. Find the probability that both are girls.
A bag holds 6 yellow and 4 blue beads. Three beads are taken without replacement. Find P(all three are blue).
Two cards are drawn from a standard deck without replacement. Find P(the first is red and the second is black).
A box has 3 mangoes and 2 oranges. Ama takes a fruit and eats it, then takes another. Draw a tree diagram and find P(she eats one mango and one orange).
